## Goal

Linearize a circuit about its DC operating point and sweep it over frequency — solve `G + jωC` at
each point, the standard SPICE AC analysis.

## Where it fits

```
 va_core::dc::OperatingPoint ──► [ac::linearize] ──► G, C
                                                     │
   .ac card + a source's AC spec ────────────────────┼──► [ac::run] ──► AcResponse{f, x}
                                                     │
                                     one complex solve per frequency
```

Downstream, `t5-acnoise/02-noise.qmd` reuses `linearize` and the very same complex solver.

## The idea

**Every device's DC-point Jacobian already *is* the small-signal conductance matrix.** No device
had to stamp anything new for this analysis to exist: `G = ∂residual/∂x` is what Newton was
already assembling, and `C = ∂charge/∂x` is what every reactive `ModelInstance` was already
stamping for T4's benefit. `ac::linearize` runs each instance's `load` at a fixed operating point
into a purpose-built `StampSink` that keeps *only* those two channels and discards the residual
and charge values themselves — DC-only quantities, meaningless once the circuit is linearized.

**The complex solve reuses the real one, by block embedding.** `CLAUDE.md` §5 restricts numerics
to `faer` and forbids adding dependencies casually, so rather than pull in a complex
linear-algebra crate, a complex system is embedded as a real one of twice the size:

```
[ G     -ω·C ] [ Re(X) ]   [ Re(B) ]
[ ω·C    G   ] [ Im(X) ] = [ Im(B) ]
```

That `2n×2n` real system goes straight to `va_core::linsolve::solve_dense` — the same dense LU
`va-core`'s own Newton loop uses. One dependency saved, one solver path shared.

**An AC source's excitation is purely a right-hand-side term.** A `VSource` already contributes a
constraint row enforcing `V(p) − V(n) = value`, and that row's Jacobian entries are already in
`G`. Its *AC magnitude and phase* are new information, but they can only ever appear in `B` — so
`ac::run` takes an `excitation` vector and places each AC-marked source's complex stimulus at its
own branch-current row. Nothing about `G`/`C` changes when the stimulus does, which is exactly
why a single linearization can serve the whole frequency sweep.

## The code

```rust
pub type Complex = (f64, f64);   // no num-complex dependency; swappable without an ABI change

pub struct AcSweep { pub fstart: f64, pub fstop: f64, pub points_per_decade: usize }
pub struct AcResponse { pub f: Vec<f64>, pub x: Vec<Vec<Complex>> }

/// Capture G and C at a fixed operating point.
pub fn linearize(instances: &[&dyn ModelInstance], x_dc: &[f64], dim: usize)
    -> (Vec<f64>, Vec<f64>);

/// Sweep, solving (G + jωC)·X = excitation at each frequency.
pub fn run(instances: &[&dyn ModelInstance], x_dc: &[f64], dim: usize,
           sweep: AcSweep, excitation: &[Complex]) -> Result<AcResponse, AcNoiseError>;
```

On the deck side, `va-netlist` learned `.ac <dec|oct|lin> <points> <fstart> <fstop>` and a `V`
line's `AC <magnitude> [phase]`. All three SPICE sweep types are accepted as of 2026-08-31
(originally `dec` only, because `AcSweep::frequencies` produced a per-decade grid and parsing a
type the analysis could not deliver would have been a promise the engine could not keep — the
fix was to implement the grids, not to loosen the parser). `points` is a *density* for `dec` and
`oct` and a *total* for `lin`, following SPICE; an unrecognized type still leaves the card
unparsed rather than being guessed at. `circuits/rc_ac_lin.net` gates the linear grid against
QSPICE — which returns exactly the 41 points the card asks for, confirming the count really is a
total on both sides.

## It works

**Against closed form first.** An RC low-pass has `H(jω) = 1/(1+jωRC)`, checked in magnitude and
phase across six decades:

```console
$ cargo test -p va-acnoise ac::
test ac::tests::rc_lowpass_response ... ok
test ac::tests::frequencies_cover_start_to_stop_at_the_requested_density ... ok
test ac::tests::frequencies_single_point_when_start_equals_stop ... ok
test ac::tests::frequencies_empty_on_a_degenerate_sweep ... ok
```

One real bug surfaced while writing those: the first `frequencies` implementation appended
`fstop` as a literal duplicate when repeated-multiplication float drift left the loop's own last
point a few ULPs short of it (`100.00000000000003` vs `100.0`). Fixed by snapping within a
relative tolerance instead of demanding bit-exact equality.

**And visibly.** `--plot` draws an AC sweep as a Bode pair (2026-08-31), magnitude in dB over
phase in degrees, sharing a logarithmic frequency axis — two panels rather than one because
decibels and degrees share neither units nor a useful scale:

```console
$ cargo run -q -p va-cli -- sim circuits/rc_ac.net --ac \
    --plot docs/tutorials/t5-acnoise/figures/rc-ac-bode.svg
```

![`rc_ac.net`'s response. `V(in)` is the 1 V source itself: flat at 0 dB and 0°, which is the
reference the other curve is read against. `V(out)` is flat below the corner, breaks at
1/(2πRC) = 159.15 Hz, and rolls off at -20 dB/decade while the phase swings from 0° toward
-90° — the single-pole shape the closed form above predicts, drawn from the same solved
response the golden gate scores.](figures/rc-ac-bode.svg)

**Then against QSPICE golden**, through two circuits chosen to separate two different claims:

```console
$ cargo run -q -p xtask -- validate
[xtask]   PASS circuits/rc_ac.net: |mag| error=1.333e-15 (tol 1e-4), phase error=1.690e-13 rad
[xtask]   PASS circuits/diode_ac.net: |mag| error=1.287e-5 (tol 1e-4), phase error=6.437e-6 rad
```

`rc_ac.net` is pure `R`/`C`/`V`, so it lands at **machine precision** — as it should, since both
simulators assemble the identical linear system. It proves the complex solve works and proves
nothing about model physics.

`diode_ac.net` is the one with teeth. It linearizes a *compiled* `models/diode.va` about a real
forward bias, so its passband gain is `1/(1 + R₁·gd)` with `gd ∝ exp(Vd/Vt)` — a **1% error in
the solved bias would move the gain by ~46%**. Agreeing to `1.3e-5` therefore constrains the DC
operating point, `va-codegen`'s AD-derived Jacobian, and the linearization that consumes it, all
at once.

### Two findings about the oracle

Neither is guessable from QSPICE's format documentation; both came from probing real runs.

**An `.ac` `.qraw` payload is not uniformly complex, despite its `Flags: complex` header.** A
5-variable, 12-point file carries 108 f64s — **9 per point, not 10**. The `Frequency` abscissa is
stored as a single *real* value, and only the remaining variables get `(re, im)` pairs. A naive
all-complex read misaligns every value after the first.

**QSPICE's frequency grid has an off-by-one at the top end.** Asked for `.ac dec 10 1 1meg` it
emits **60** points: `10^(k/10)` for `k = 0..=58`, then a jump straight to `fstop`, silently
dropping `10^5.9 ≈ 794.3 kHz`. The mathematically clean grid — 10 per decade, both endpoints
included — is 61. Rather than teach this project's sweep to reproduce someone else's off-by-one,
`va_harness::ac::compare_ac` **matches by frequency**: every golden point is looked up in the
computed sweep and compared there exactly. No interpolation is involved, because the grids
genuinely coincide wherever they overlap — unlike the transient case, where two adaptive
integrators share no timebase at all and resampling is unavoidable.

### The metric is two numbers, not one

`CLAUDE.md` §7 states the AC metric as "magnitude/phase error within a stated band," which is
genuinely **two** bands. `compare_ac` returns separate verdicts for each rather than collapsing
them, because a magnitude that tracks golden while the phase drifts is a different bug (a wrong
reactive/charge stamp) from the reverse (a wrong conductance) — and one combined number would
hide which happened.

Phase needs two guards the other metrics don't. Differences are wrapped into `(−π, π]`, so a
reference sitting on the ±180° branch cut — `rc_ac.net`'s own `I(V1)` approaches `−180°` at high
frequency — doesn't report a ~2π "error" for a negligible disagreement. And points whose
reference magnitude is below the noise floor are skipped entirely, since the phase of a value at
both simulators' round-off floor is arbitrary.

```console
$ cargo test -p va-harness ac::
test ac::tests::run_ac_solves_the_rc_lowpass ... ok
test ac::tests::compare_ac_reports_magnitude_and_phase_failures_separately ... ok
test ac::tests::compare_ac_tolerates_a_computed_sweep_with_extra_frequencies ... ok
test ac::tests::compare_ac_errors_when_a_golden_frequency_is_missing ... ok
test ac::tests::compare_ac_passes_for_an_identical_reference ... ok
test ac::tests::compare_ac_rejects_a_node_order_mismatch ... ok
test ac::tests::run_ac_errors_on_a_deck_with_no_ac_card ... ok
```

## Limitations

- **`dec` sweeps only** — no `lin` or `oct` grid, as above.
- **The dense solve is `O(n³)` per frequency point.** Fine at zoo scale; the sparse-solve backlog
  item in `docs/roadmap.md` would lift it for both AC and DC together, since they share
  `linsolve`.
- **A deck with no AC-marked source is an error**, not a zero answer. The system would be
  homogeneous and solve to identically zero at every frequency — a silently useless result, so
  `va-cli` refuses it instead.
- **No AC-specific device behavior**: what gets linearized is whatever `load` stamps. A model with
  frequency-dependent physics beyond `G + jωC` has no way to express it through Interface β.

## What's next

`t5-acnoise/02-noise.qmd` — the noise analysis this linearization feeds, which reuses `linearize`
and the same block-embedded solver, and needed one genuinely new thing from every device.
